implementation_notes: Moq fabricates the double at runtime from the interface or virtual class: new Mock<IClock>() is configured with mock.Setup(c => c.Now).Returns(v), .Throws(new TimeoutException()), .Callback(...) or SetupSequence(...).Returns(a).Returns(b).Throws(e) for successive calls, and mock.Object is handed to the SUT; MockBehavior.Strict turns unconfigured calls into failures while the default loose behaviour returns defaults. Because configurations are lambda expressions, the compiler checks the member and its arguments, replacing the hand-written configuration interface.
pitfalls: Loose mocks (the default) answer unconfigured calls with defaults, so a test can pass without ever exercising the intended path; use MockBehavior.Strict or VerifyNoOtherCalls to catch that.
Recursive mocks (DefaultValue.Mock) return a new configured mock for chains that were never set up, hiding a missing setup behind a green test.
Configurations live on the instance, so a mock reused across tests must be re-created or Reset() or previously recorded setups leak forward.

variants.name: Hand-written fake class with delegate properties
variants.idiom_name: test-local class implementing the interface with Func<T> members
variants.implementation_notes: A reusable fake implements the collaborator interface and exposes one delegate or settable property per member that the test assigns in fixture setup, so throwing is expressed by assigning a delegate that throws and the class stays a normal C# type that the compiler checks. Prefer it when the test project must not take a mocking dependency, when the interface is small, or when the fake needs real logic such as a call counter; the toolkit form wins once the interface is wide or the test needs argument matching.
pitfalls: The fake is mutable state shared by tests unless each test constructs its own; a property assigned in one test survives into the next when the fixture is shared.
Assigning only some delegates leaves the default answers active, which is the hand-written equivalent of a loose mock silently passing.

Explicit interface implementation keeps the configuration surface (the delegate properties) invisible to the SUT only if the SUT is typed as the interface; a concrete-typed fake exposes both surfaces.

variants.name: System.Reflection.DispatchProxy proxy driven by a response table
variants.idiom_name: DispatchProxy subclass with a configured method-name response table
variants.implementation_notes: DispatchProxy.Create<T, TProxy>() fabricates an interface implementation at runtime and routes every call to Invoke(MethodInfo, object[]), so a generated proxy class plus a dictionary of configured return values or expected arguments is a fully dynamic configurable double built from the platform itself. This is the mechanism that mocking toolkits sit on; write it by hand only when the double needs cross-cutting behaviour a toolkit cannot express, such as a proxy that also records a policy decision.
pitfalls: Dispatch is name- and reflection-based: properties arrive as get_/set_ methods, so a renamed member silently stops matching the response table.
A proxy is created per interface type and cached, so configured state must live on the instance; storing it in statics leaks between tests and between concurrent test runners.
Reflection adds per-call overhead and defeats ahead-of-time/trimming scenarios, which matters if the test doubles are used on a trimmed or AOT target.
